tagline: A canyon tunnel once carried a sixty-foot painting above its entrance.
intro: Malibu Canyon-Las Virgenes Highway connects the Santa Monica Mountains with Pacific Coast Highway at Pepperdine University. The drive includes a tunnel cut beneath a rock face in Malibu Canyon. Caltrans records the section from Route 1 to Lost Hills Road as an officially designated County Scenic Highway, recognized in 2002.

In 1966, that tunnel became the setting for an unusual roadside art dispute. Artist Lynne Seemayer spent nights suspended on ropes removing graffiti above its southern entrance, then painted a sixty-foot nude on the cleared rock. County road officials feared traffic problems and tried to wash the painting away. When removal failed, a crew covered it with brown paint on November 3, less than a week after its creation.

Traveling south from Lost Hills Road, the corridor leads toward the Malibu Hindu Temple, off Malibu Canyon Road in the Santa Monica Mountains. Farther south comes the tunnel, followed by Pepperdine and the junction with Pacific Coast Highway. At the coast, the Malibu Bluffs Recreation Area lies directly opposite the university and canyon road, above Amarillo and Puerco beaches.

moments.title: Malibu Hindu Temple
moments.text: Two temples occupy the complex: Venkateswara presides in the upper temple and Shiva in the lower one. Their concrete construction follows the Dravidian architectural style of South India. Smaller shrines honor Rama, Lakshmi, Bhoodevi, Krishna and Hanuman. Construction began in 1981, and the complex serves Hindu worship and cultural events in Southern California. The Hindu Temple Society of Southern California maintains the temple, where priests perform daily rituals and special ceremonies. The complex stands in the Santa Monica Mountains in Calabasas, off Malibu Canyon Road near the city of Malibu.

moments.title: Malibu Canyon tunnel
moments.text: The rock above the tunnel’s southern entrance once held the Pink Lady, a sixty-foot nude painted by Lynne Seemayer. She completed it on October 28, 1966, after months spent clearing graffiti from the rock. Local news coverage gave the painting its name because of the pink paint used for the figure’s skin. Her heavy-duty house paint resisted both fire hoses and paint stripper. Seemayer sought a court injunction to save the work, but the attempt failed. A road crew painted over it on November 3. The figure showed through the fading brown paint for years before it was finally removed.

moments.title: Malibu
moments.text: At the canyon road’s meeting with Pacific Coast Highway, Pepperdine occupies a campus outside Malibu’s city limits. The university expanded to Malibu in 1972, and asked to remain outside the boundaries when the city incorporated in 1991. Its hillside buildings use white stucco walls and red tile roofs. Across the highway, Malibu Bluffs Recreation Area occupies the bluffs above Amarillo and Puerco beaches. The recreation area surrounds Malibu Bluffs Community Park, linking the canyon’s coastal endpoint with a landscape of bluffs and shoreline. Pepperdine’s Phillips Theme Tower is a 125-foot obelisk with an embedded cross, completed in 1973.
